Circle Square Circle

GeometryCirclesArea
Game: A circle sits inside a square, with a turning square and a smaller circle inside it, and a small square and circle fit under two curves. Drag the dots and see what keeps touching.
How to play: Drag a labelled dot, or focus it and use the arrow keys. Slide the angle to turn a square, and use the buttons to start again or show the exact fit.

The gothic cupola: drag A, B, G or O.

The applet's picture: drag O, A2 or B, or slide the angle.

5°
Look for the math

One picture has squares and circles tucked inside each other; the other hides a pair of fractions. Turn the square and the tangencies never change.

A square, a circle, a square, a circle

Start with a square A. Draw the circle C that touches its four sides. A square B fits inside C, and a smaller circle fits inside B. If C has radius R, then B has side R√2 and its incircle has radius R/√2. So the inner circle's area is exactly half the outer circle's:

π (R/√2)² = πR² / 2

Why turning changes nothing

The corners of B sit on C at angles 45° + θ, 135° + θ, and so on. The distance from the shared centre to any side of B is its corner's radius times cos 45°, which is always R/√2. That is exactly the small circle's radius, so every side of B is tangent to it, whatever the angle. The applet's scroll bar runs from 0 to 50 degrees and starts at 5; the logic test checks all 51 positions on many board sizes. At exactly 45 degrees the applet also draws two lines through the midpoints of A's sides: a harmless quirk of its drawing code, not part of the rule.

The cupola on the linked page

The cut-the-knot page filed under this applet's name shows a different picture: two quarter circles in a square of side S form a gothic cupola, a small square of side x sits below, and a circle of radius r rests on it. Its corner G lies on a quarter circle, so by the Pythagorean theorem, (S/2 + x/2)² + x² = S². That gives 5x² + 2Sx − 3S² = 0, with the positive root x = 3S/5. The circle touches the curved roof too: (S/2)² + (x + r)² = (S − r)², which with x = 3S/5 gives r = 39S/320. The logic test confirms both fractions for hundreds of sizes. No applet is embedded on that page (checked the live page, its links and archived copies), so it is cited here as the closest verified article; the drawing follows the applet's own code.

Try Turn to 45° and drag A2 outward: the little circle stays tangent. Then drag G away from the fit and press Show exact fit to bring back both fractions.
